This game is amazing and really engaging. I ended up completing the entire game, including the Labyrinth DLC, in under two days. The concept is very creative, the puzzles are well-designed, and I really dig the overall aesthetic.

Now, on to the bad stuff:
1. The UI and graphics feel slightly broken. Depending on the font size you choose in the settings, text can overflow or end up with incorrect alignment and padding. Fullscreen mode also sometimes feels unreliable, and the lack of borderless mode doesn’t help.
2. I’m not a fan of the secondary terminal that launches alongside the game. I’m not sure whether it’s a technical limitation or a design choice, but either way it feels out of place and a bit unprofessional, and it also interferes with Alt+Tab.
3. There’s no SFX volume slider—you can only adjust the music volume.
4. As the game progresses and you discover more nodes, it becomes quite difficult to keep track of what’s what, even after unlocking that one program in the DLC that helps organize the node layout. A better navigation system (or something as simple as querying for already discovered nodes by name) would go a long way.

Overall, the base game and its DLC are definitely worth picking up, and I hope Matt releases a new DLC or a sequel soon.

I just finished this game, and I had a great time. 

I've played a few hacker-sim games over the years, and this is the first one I felt like I could dig my teeth into. It wasn't terribly overwhelming in terms of the tutorial or game mechanics like most other hacker games, but most of you hacking involves typing commands into a fake terminal, so you do feel like a movie-style hacker.  This is enhanced by a phenomenal soundtrack and a well-designed HUD.  

I particularly like that programs that you run are added to a window on the HUD that represents your RAM usage, and when you run a program (porthack, SSHcrack, etc) take up the amount of space in the window as how much RAM it's using. Might not make a lot of sense typing it out, but essentially you can visually see how much total RAM you have vs the amount of RAM whatever you're running at any given time. You kind of have to play it to fully get what I mean, but it can add a lot of tension when you're watching a passive trace count down with the next hack command in the terminal just WAITING for the previous hack to complete so you can activate it. 

The story is also really interesting, and there are lots of little fun things to find in the files of the devices you hack into if you dig around and read txt and IRC files. There's even a functional clicker game you can play!

The game is fairly short: a 10-15 hour story, but it's really interesting and fun do dive into. I did have to look up a walkthrough a couple times, but once I read the solution, I realized it was something incredibly obvious that I just missed or forgot to do.  I recently started my second playthrough, and I'm excited to find secrets I ignored or missed during my first playthrough. 

If you want to feel like a 1337 haxorz pr0 this is the game for you.  It was made by a handful of people, but is bursting with personality and interesting design. This is probably going to be added to my rotation of games to replay every year. 

(Seriously tho, check out the IRC Logs. There's some funny shit in there)

[i]Such[/i] an incredible game! Hacknet is the medium-high tension Hollywood hacker sim that I wanted when I first played Introversion's [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1510/Uplink/]Uplink[/url], but this time with an engaging (and heartfelt!) story. Emulating real Unix terminal syntax interspersed with spicy blackbox command-line executables, the game immerses players in the world of characters they barely interact with outside of emails [spoiler]or the occasional counter-hack[/spoiler]. And yet, digging into the notes and logs and data found on servers and mainframes here and there, we get to see more facets of these anonymous (and sometimes strange) people's lives, even if their stories never achieve full clarity.

Hacknet was clearly made with a goal in mind, a narrative vision, and a lot of love. I can't wait to get started with its DLC, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/521840/Hacknet__Labyrinths/?curator_clanid=9425916]Labyrinths[/url]. I can see myself coming back to this gem time and time again.

Hacknet is one of those games that really pulls you in with its atmosphere and style. The core gameplay is solid and feels great—there’s a real sense of pressure while you’re navigating systems, cracking passwords, and racing against time. It does a great job of making you feel like you’re actually “in” the terminal, and that immersion is a big part of why it works so well.

The music fits perfectly. It’s not over the top, but it builds tension in just the right moments and keeps you focused. Combined with the pacing, it really enhances that feeling of urgency and keeps you engaged.

Overall, after playing for a longer stretch, the tasks can start to feel a bit repetitive. You’ll notice similar patterns in missions, which can take away some of the excitement over time. Still, it doesn’t completely ruin the experience—it just makes it better enjoyed in shorter sessions.

Overall, Hacknet is a really good game that I keep coming back to every now and then. Even with some repetition, the atmosphere, music, and gameplay loop make it worth revisiting. <3

Additionally, there are a good bunch of extensions available on the Workshop of the game, which are made by enthusiasts and it really shows. To summarize, the whole experience from A to Z is pretty much a 10/10 on a casual games basis, where you'd like to relax but challenge yourself a bit, regarding problemsolving and some detective kinda stuff.

Hacknet is a game I played a long time ago (probably pirated) as a kid, and I could never get it out of my head. About ten years later I saw it on sale for TWO (Yes two) dollars and bought it right away.

I ended up playing it nonstop and it felt like I never stopped playing. The game throws you in and there is a lot to remember, but it is very intuitive and immersive once you get used to it. It took me about 7 hours to finish the game and around 9.5 hours to get all the achievements.

What makes it special is how advanced it feels for its time. It could have just been a simple text based hacking game, but instead it feels like a full operating system with a story and characters you grow attached to even though you never see them.

The Pacemaker mission was very memorable. The music goes dead silent for a while with this quiet droning as it goes on before the normal relaxing music comes back after a few minutes. The ETAS system also scared me when I connected to the honeypot server but was so fun to bypass & mess with!

Hacknet is a solid game and I had tons of fun with it. I found the game on a deal, quite cheap and, although I have never played something similar, it hooked me and I finished it in two sits. 

I don't know anything about hacking or programming but I am drawn to these topics in fiction, so if you like a good narrative about hacking then this game is good for that. You don't need to have any specialised knowledge and the mechanics of the game are pretty straightforward, not super complicated but fun enough. 

Some people in the review comments say the levels and how to go through them is a bit repetitive - I can understand the feeling but the progression is ok and, for the duration of the game, just enough. 

So, overall, I think the main strength of the game is its narrative, and the mechanics are good enough to make you feel like you are hacking, independently of how close is to the real thing. Definitely recommended!
